A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SD-SCM research. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support comparison, including material moved from the main text into appendices.

before.justification: V1 reports original simulations, treatment-effect estimation experiments on GPT-2- and Llama-3-8b-generated datasets, and an empirical illustration of language-model auditing.

after.justification: V2 retains original empirical results and adds larger-sample estimation experiments, additional baseline results, and a sample-size comparison.

M1.justification: The specified counterfactual procedure changes from preserving observed ancestors of the intervened variable in v1 Definition 9 to preserving observed non-descendants in v2 Definition A.9 and Algorithms 1/4. This can change counterfactual sampling on general DAGs. The underlying SD-SCM framework remains intact; the added pseudocode otherwise mainly documents existing procedures.

E1.justification: Both versions use the gym/weather confounder-versus-collider example and the same 14-variable breast-cancer simulation for ATE, CATE, ITE estimation and model auditing. Observed- and hidden-covariate settings remain. The larger datasets change sample size, not domain or task coverage.

E2.justification: V2 adds LinearS, LinearT, ForestS, and ForestT to the reported ATE and CATE/ITE comparisons. LinReg and RF remain separate entries, so these additions are not merely renamings. V2's toy-example Figure 2 also drops the mean-difference baseline displayed in v1 Figure 2.

E3.justification: V2 adds evaluations on 10,000-observation datasets aggregated within each SD-SCM variation and makes this the main CATE/ITE setting, while retaining 1,000-observation evaluations in Appendix C. This substantially changes the sample-size conditions supporting the central evaluation. The toy example also revises its stated weather and marathon phrasings.

E4.justification: V2 Appendix C.2, Table 2, and Figure 8 introduce a substantive sample-size sensitivity analysis across both language models and both covariate settings. It directly tests whether estimation difficulties arise only from small samples, a question v1's fixed-size evaluation did not address. The confounder/collider demonstration and interval case studies already existed.

E5.justification: Both versions describe 50 SD-SCM variations with 20 generated datasets per variation and evaluate effect intervals using nominal 95% coverage and standardized widths. V2 extends these reporting practices to larger datasets without adding seed disclosures, repeated-run counts, significance tests, or a new uncertainty-estimation procedure.

E6.justification: V2 adds S/T-learner results and extensive 10,000-sample R2, coverage, and PEHE results. Its new Table 2 reports, for example, Llama-3-8b BART mean R2 of 0.5221 at 1,000 observations versus 0.9214 at 10,000 with all covariates; these compare sample-size conditions, not same-setting improvements between versions. All original Table 1 entries are retained unchanged. Toy-example plot values change, and the original 1,000-sample PEHE plots are replaced by 10,000-sample plots.

T1.justification: Beyond relocating definitions to Appendix A, v2 changes the parent-only concatenation definition to append the current variable's sequence and broadens the counterfactual evidence set from ancestors to non-descendants. These are mathematical specification changes. Most definitions and the PEHE formulas remain unchanged, and no new theorem or proof is introduced.

C1.justification: The framework, benchmark, and auditing applications remain the core contributions. V2 adds explicit headline conclusions that causal methods outperform non-causal methods and that individualized estimation challenges even state-of-the-art methods, suggesting inherent estimation difficulties. V1's abstract primarily announces the framework and experimental comparisons.

C2.justification: V2 explicitly frames hidden-U evaluation as testing violations of identification assumptions, interprets the sample-size results as evidence against a purely small-sample explanation, and identifies manual management of phrasing sensitivity as a limitation. Existing discussion of dependence on LM-encoded mechanisms is largely retained or relocated. V1's specific qualification that the breast-cancer simulation need not reflect medically accurate relationships is removed, although v2 adds broader inaccuracy caveats.

D1.justification: V2 adds explicit observational, interventional, and counterfactual sampling pseudocode and discloses V100 and RTX8000 GPU use in Appendix B. These improve procedural and hardware documentation. The repository/data-access information and policy of using default estimator implementations remain.

R1.justification: V2 adds Ravfogel et al. (2024) and a focused comparison with that work and Chatzi et al. (2024), distinguishing semantic interventions and user-controlled DAGs from interventions within language models. It also removes several general ATE references, including Rubin, Lalonde, and Imai. Most related-work positioning is retained.

P1.justification: V2 extensively rewrites the introduction around a worked toy example and numbered contributions, condenses the main methods exposition, moves formal definitions and detailed ATE reporting into appendices, and adds a separate Limitations section. The results narrative is reorganized around the larger-sample evaluation. This substantially changes the paper's explanatory structure.

P2.justification: V2 changes to a two-column layout, redraws the overview and clinical DAGs, and combines the toy-example diagrams and results into a redesigned Figure 2. It relocates the expanded ATE table and example-data figure, adds algorithm displays and the sample-size table/chart, and reorganizes estimation plots between the main text and appendices.

improvement.justification: The sample-size comparison strengthens validation by testing an important alternative explanation for v1's estimation difficulties. The worked example, sampling pseudocode, and identification discussion also improve clarity. The gain is qualified: the stronger interpretation of inherent difficulty still rests on default estimator configurations, and the explicit medical-accuracy qualification is lost. Overall, the added control and clearer documentation provide an evidence-supported improvement.
